strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple modalities (image, audio, video, human motion) with appropriate evaluation metrics and consistent improvements
Clear practical value: parameter-free, plug-and-play approach requiring no external models or data, achieving 8.75× speedup and 23.6% FID improvement
Well-motivated problem identifying real limitations of existing guidance methods (external dependency, computational overhead)
Solid experimental methodology with ablation studies on layer selection, λ sensitivity, and robustness analysis across architectures
Practical applicability across different domains and network architectures without domain-specific modifications
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is a straightforward regularization term (cosine similarity of patch-wise features) that is incremental rather than conceptually novel
Lacks theoretical understanding of why layer alignment improves generation quality; the mechanism is described empirically but not rigorously analyzed
Unfair experimental comparisons: Table 1 compares at different iteration counts, Table 3 uses different epoch counts for baseline vs LayerSync, limiting comparisons with other guidance methods

Heuristic-driven design choices without principled justification: layer selection strategy (excluding final 20%, minimum distance of 8 blocks) appears arbitrary; no ablation on why cosine similarity is optimal
Overclaimed simplicity: method described as 'parameter-free' but includes hyperparameter λ requiring tuning; different λ values (0.2, 0.3) used across experiments with unclear selection criteria
Statistical rigor issues: most main results lack confidence intervals or significance tests; improvements are often modest (e.g., 20.7% audio FAD improvement)
Video experiments showing less impressive improvements (19.1%, 22.8%) relegated to appendix; limited testing beyond SiT-based architectures
Incomplete mechanistic analysis: why should aligning shallow and deep representations improve generation quality? The claimed 'homogeneous feature distribution' is stated but not proven

strengths: Comprehensive multi-domain experimental validation (image, audio, video, human motion) demonstrating broad applicability and consistent improvements across diverse generative tasks
Strong empirical results with significant practical impact: 8.75× training acceleration on ImageNet, 23.6% FID improvement, and consistent gains across all tested domains
Well-motivated approach using self-alignment as intrinsic guidance, avoiding dependency on external models while achieving competitive or superior results to external guidance methods
Thorough ablation studies and robustness analysis including layer selection experiments (Table 5), hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 6), and block-dropping experiments demonstrating method stability
Practical advantages with plug-and-play integration, no additional trainable parameters, low computational overhead, and clear applicability across different architectures and modalities
High-quality analysis of learned representations with PCA visualizations, attention map comparisons, and quantitative metrics (32.4% classification accuracy improvement) supporting the core claims
Excellent reproducibility with commitment to open-source release, comprehensive implementation details in appendices, detailed hyperparameter specifications, and clear algorithmic descriptions
Clear and well-organized presentation with effective figures and tables that clearly communicate the method's effectiveness and design choices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty as the core idea builds on well-established representation alignment work; the main contribution is applying layer-wise alignment to diffusion models specifically, which is incremental
Insufficient theoretical justification for why layer-wise alignment improves generation quality; the connection is demonstrated empirically but lacks theoretical grounding or mechanistic explanation

Layer selection strategy is somewhat ad-hoc with the minimum distance heuristic (8 blocks for SiT-XL, 3 for SiT-B) lacking principled justification and potentially requiring architecture-specific tuning

Despite claims of being parameter-free, hyperparameter λ still requires tuning with different values used across experiments (0.2-0.3 range); could be more explicit about default recommendations and sensitivity
Insufficient analysis of failure cases, limitations, and edge cases; paper would benefit from explicitly discussing when LayerSync might underperform or provide minimal improvements

Representation learning analysis in Section 4.4 is relatively brief; deeper investigation into what properties of aligned representations improve generation quality would strengthen mechanistic understanding
Video generation experiments relegated to appendix with limited scope (24k steps on CLEVERER for from-scratch, primarily fine-tuning results); broader validation would strengthen multi-modal claims
Statistical rigor could be improved with more extensive error reporting; while ablations include standard deviations, main comparisons lack confidence intervals and explicit significance testing
Computational overhead claims could be more prominent with per-step cost explicitly stated in main text rather than appendix; efficiency gains appear to come primarily from faster convergence
Limited comparison with recent alternative representation guidance methods beyond Dispersive Loss; broader exploration of the guidance method landscape would provide better positioning

strengths: Comprehensive cross-domain evaluation demonstrating applicability to image, audio, video, and human motion generation
Practical self-contained method requiring no external models or additional data, with clear reproducibility commitment
Consistent and significant empirical improvements (8.75× training acceleration on ImageNet, 23.6% quality improvement)
Thorough ablation studies examining layer selection, λ coefficient, block dropping, and learning rate effects
Detailed experimental setup with well-documented hyperparameters and commitment to open-source code
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: represents an incremental application of well-established representation alignment principles to diffusion models, lacking technical innovation
Weak theoretical justification for why alignment helps; 'virtuous cycle' hypothesis is speculative rather than rigorously validated, and gradient norm analysis confuses correlation with mechanism

Ad-hoc layer selection heuristic (exclude last 20%, exclude first layers, minimum 8-block distance) lacks principled justification and provides limited guidance for practitioners applying to new architectures
Unfair experimental comparisons: Table 1 compares Dispersive Loss at 160 epochs to SiT-XL+LayerSync at 800 epochs, conflating training duration with method contribution
Insufficient mechanistic analysis: paper does not adequately investigate whether improvements stem from better representations, optimization dynamics, or implicit regularization
Limited architectural diversity: image generation experiments only use SiT models; no evaluation on U-Net variants, DiT, or other popular diffusion model architectures
Incomplete baseline comparisons: only one self-contained baseline (Dispersive Loss) for image generation; audio/motion comparisons primarily against non-comparable external guidance methods
Design choices lack justification: asymmetric stopgrad in Eq. 2 unexplained; cosine similarity chosen without comparison to alternative alignment losses (MSE, KL divergence)

Dense presentation obscures insights; Algorithm 1 is trivially simple (compute negative similarity) despite extensive motivation; Section 3.2 on block structure feels disconnected from main contribution
Insufficient analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity beyond λ coefficient; multiple design thresholds (layer distances, block exclusions) with limited ablation

strengths: Comprehensive cross-modal evaluation demonstrating domain-agnostic applicability: consistent improvements on image, audio, human motion, and video generation with substantial speedups (8.75× on ImageNet 256×256)
Significant practical improvements with strong empirical results: 23.6% FID improvement on ImageNet, 20.7% FAD improvement on audio, and 7.7% FID improvement on human motion generation

Extensive ablation studies validating design choices: comprehensive analysis of layer selection (Tables 11-12), regularization coefficient sensitivity (Table 7), block dropping effects (Table 9), and gradient dynamics (Figure 7)
Well-motivated approach grounded in observations of representation quality hierarchy: the self-alignment principle is intuitive and empirically validated through representation analysis in Section G
Parameter-free, plug-and-play solution requiring no external models or additional data: easily adoptable by practitioners and composable with other methods (e.g., REPA)

Strong representation learning analysis: Section G provides compelling empirical evidence for the 'virtuous cycle' hypothesis, showing how internal alignment propagates improvements through the model hierarchy
Excellent reproducibility and clarity: detailed experimental procedures, rigorous methodology, and commitment to open-source all code and configurations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core technique (aligning normalized representations via cosine similarity) is straightforward and standard; the main contribution is identifying where to apply it rather than proposing novel methodology

Layer selection strategy lacks principled justification: the heuristic choices (exclude final 20%, exclude first layers, enforce 8-block distance) are empirically motivated without theoretical grounding; generalization to non-transformer architectures unclear
Incomplete computational overhead analysis: claims of 'negligible overhead' (abstract) lack quantification; no FLOPs breakdown or detailed timing analysis of LayerSync loss computation provided

Limited theoretical understanding of why the method works: while Section G provides empirical evidence, the paper lacks theoretical analysis of the optimization dynamics and convergence mechanisms underlying the improvement
Moderate hyperparameter sensitivity without clear guidance: λ robustness spans FID 36.19→31.36 (Table 7); no principled approach provided for selecting λ on new domains or tasks
Statistical significance under-reported: most results lack error bars; standard deviations in Table 6 (±0.8) are non-negligible relative to claimed improvements
Limited comparison with recent concurrent work: primary baseline is Dispersive Loss; insufficient comparison with other recent self-supervised regularization and representation learning methods
Underdeveloped video generation experiments: only 2 datasets tested despite claimed domain-agnosticity; video results relegated to appendix despite being integral to cross-modal claims
Unexplained discrepancy in audio results: 20.7% FAD improvement substantially exceeds image FID improvements (~10-12%), but paper does not discuss why or investigate this difference
Unclear architectural generalization: experiments on compact 8-layer models; scalability to very large models (100+ layers), CNNs, and other architectures not adequately addressed
